vignette:
Carlos is a 26-year-old man who came to his first session with a careful, almost rehearsed posture. He sits at the edge of the armchair, his hands resting flat on his thighs, his eyes scanning the room before settling on the door. He arrives to therapy straight from his shift at a downtown hotel, where he works as a maid. The lavender smell of industrial cleaner still clings to his uniform, and he apologizes for it twice before I reassure him it’s fine.

He tells his story in fragments at first. Two years ago, he lived in a small city in Central America. He had finished high school and was working at a copy shop, saving money to help his mother. One evening, after closing the shop, three men in civilian clothes pulled him into a van. They accused him of distributing opposition flyers—flyers he had only copied for a customer, never read. For three days they held him in a concrete room. They burned his arms with a cigarette lighter. They wrapped a plastic bag over his head until he lost consciousness. They waterboarded him. They told him they would find his mother if he ever spoke.

Carlos describes this in a low, even voice, as if reading a script. He does not look at me when he says the words. His fingers are still resting motionless on his thighs. He was released on the third night, thrown onto a dirt road with a broken collarbone and two cracked ribs. He did not go to the hospital. He did not tell his mother the full truth. Within two weeks, he fled to the United States, where a cousin helped him get a job at the hotel.

Now, he works double shifts when he can. The days are safer than the nights. He spends his cleaning cart around the hallways, avoiding the elevator because the confined space makes his chest tighten. He only uses the stairs, counting the landings under his breath. He flinches when a guest touches him on the shoulder to get his attention. Once, a child left a clear plastic shower cap on the bathroom sink, and he stood in the doorway for three full minutes before he could step inside. The shape of it—the way it lay flat and transparent—reminded him of the bag.

At home, he lives alone in a small studio. He sleeps with the light on and wedges a chair under the doorknob. He does not answer the phone unless he knows the number. He divorced his wife eight months ago. She could not understand why he would not hold her at night, why he woke up swinging, why he could not bear the sound of the shower running in the other room. He tells me he loved her. He still does. But when she touched his back, he saw the concrete room. He felt the plastic. He pushed her away and kept pushing until she left.

Carlos has nightmares almost every night. In the worst one, he is back in the room, but the men have his mother’s faces. He wakes up gasping, his sheets soaked. During the day, he feels like he is watching himself from a distance—pushing the cart, folding towels, nodding at guests. That numb space is the only relief. But it does not last. He avoids news from his country. He cannot watch movies with closed rooms or dark windows. He has lost fifteen pounds because eating feels like swallowing stones.

When I ask what he hopes for, he laughs for the first time—a short, dry sound. He says he hopes the cleaning supply closet at work stays unlocked so he does not have to panic in the hallway. He says he hopes his mother never tells him the truth about what happened after he left. He says he does not remember wanting anything before the van. Then he stops talking, and we sit in silence for a long moment. Outside, a door clicks shut down the hall, and Carlos flinches—a full-body recoil, knees pulling up, hands flying to his chest. He recovers in a second, apologizing again, but his eyes stay fixed on the door.
